prompt: β-Oxidation step 1 turns a fatty acyl CoA into a trans-enoyl CoA (a C=C forms). Which coenzyme is used?
why: ATP activates the fatty acid before β-oxidation. It doesn’t remove hydrogens.
NADPH is a reducing agent for synthesis. β-Oxidation is an oxidation.
NAD+ oxidizes alcohols to ketones (step 3 of β-oxidation), not C–C to C=C.
hint: A C=C forms.
explain: Making a C=C from C–C is FAD’s job; FAD becomes FADH<sub style="font-size:13.8667px;line-height:0px">2</sub>.

prompt: A –CH2–CH2– becomes –CH=CH– (succinate → fumarate). Which coenzyme takes the hydrogens?
why: NAD+ handles C–O oxidations (alcohol → ketone). Making a C=C from C–C uses FAD.
ATP carries phosphate groups and energy, not hydrogens.
NADH is already reduced, so it can’t take more hydrogens.
hint: Which coenzyme makes C=C bonds?
explain: FAD oxidizes (dehydrogenates) an alkane section to an alkene and is reduced to FADH<sub style="font-size:13.8667px;line-height:0px">2</sub>.

prompt: Which coenzyme is a phosphate group carrier?
why: Coenzyme A carries acyl and acetyl groups.
NAD+ carries hydrogens and electrons.
FAD carries hydrogens and electrons.
hint: Kinases use it.
explain: ATP donates phosphate groups (and energy) in phosphorylation reactions.

prompt: Yeast reduce acetaldehyde to ethanol. Which coenzyme supplies the hydrogens?
why: Coenzyme A carries acyl groups and isn’t a reducing agent.
NAD+ is what forms. It can’t supply hydrogens.
FAD is an oxidizing agent. Here acetaldehyde is reduced, so something must give hydrogens.
hint: Reduction needs a reducing agent.
explain: NADH reduces the aldehyde and is recycled to NAD+ so glycolysis can continue.

prompt: A 2° alcohol is oxidized to a ketone (malate → oxaloacetate). Which coenzyme takes the hydrogens?
why: Coenzyme A carries acetyl and acyl groups. It isn’t an oxidizing agent.
NADPH is a reducing agent for building molecules. It gives hydrogens; it doesn’t take them.
FAD oxidizes C–C to C=C. Oxidizing an alcohol (C–O) to a ketone uses NAD+.
hint: Which coenzyme handles C–O bonds?
explain: NAD+ is the oxidizing agent for C–O oxidations: 2° alcohol → ketone. It is reduced to NADH + H+.

prompt: A ketone is reduced to an alcohol while a fatty acid is being built (lipogenesis). Which coenzyme supplies the hydrogens?
why: NADH supplies hydrogens in catabolism (for example pyruvate → lactate). Biosynthesis uses NADPH.
FADH<sub style="font-size:13.8667px;line-height:0px">2</sub> passes its electrons to the electron transport chain. It isn’t used to reduce ketones in synthesis.
NAD+ is an oxidizing agent: it takes hydrogens. This step needs a reducing agent.
hint: Building pathways use the phosphorylated version.
explain: Biosynthesis (anabolism) uses NADPH as its reducing agent; NADPH comes from the pentose phosphate pathway.

prompt: Muscle reduces pyruvate to lactate. Which coenzyme supplies the hydrogens?
why: FAD is an oxidizing agent. Here pyruvate is reduced, so something must give hydrogens.
NAD+ is what forms. It takes hydrogens; it can’t supply them.
NADPH is the reducing agent for biosynthesis, not for lactate fermentation.
hint: A reducing agent is in its reduced form.
explain: NADH is the reducing agent: it gives up its H and becomes NAD+, which glycolysis needs to keep running.

prompt: Glycerol 3-phosphate is oxidized to dihydroxyacetone phosphate by NAD+. What happens to the NAD+?
why: Coenzymes like NAD+ are changed in the reaction and have to be recycled; the enzyme is the catalyst.
NADPH is a different coenzyme (it has an extra phosphate). NAD+ becomes NADH.
Gaining hydrogens (NAD+ → NADH) is reduction, not oxidation.
hint: Gaining H = reduction.
explain: NAD+ is the oxidizing agent, so it gains H and is reduced to NADH. A dehydrogenase enzyme does this.

prompt: Glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate is oxidized in glycolysis step 6. Which coenzyme is the oxidizing agent?
why: FADH<sub style="font-size:13.8667px;line-height:0px">2</sub> is reduced and comes from the citric acid cycle and β-oxidation, not glycolysis.
NADH is the reduced form. It is what forms here, not the oxidizing agent.
Coenzyme A carries acyl groups and isn’t an oxidizing agent.
hint: The oxidizing agent is in its oxidized form.
explain: NAD+ accepts the hydrogens and becomes NADH; this is where glycolysis makes its 2 NADH.

Ethanol is oxidized by NAD+ in the liver (alcohol dehydrogenase). What is the first product?
why: A ketone needs a C=O in the middle of the chain. Ethanol is a 1° alcohol, so it gives an aldehyde.
That removes the –OH (a reduction). Oxidation makes a C=O.
That is dehydration (losing water), not oxidation by NAD+.
explain: A 1° alcohol is oxidized to an aldehyde first (further oxidation gives acetic acid).

explain: Water splits arginine into urea and ornithine, which goes back into the mitochondria to start the cycle again.

explain: The 2° alcohol becomes a ketone: dihydroxyacetone phosphate, which can enter glycolysis or gluconeogenesis.

prompt: A triacylglycerol is completely hydrolyzed (lipoprotein lipase). What are the products?
why: That is incomplete hydrolysis, as pancreatic lipase does in the intestine. Complete hydrolysis breaks all three esters.

The backbone is glycerol, not glucose. Hydrolysis frees glycerol.
explain: Complete hydrolysis breaks all three ester bonds. (Pancreatic lipase in the intestine does an incomplete hydrolysis: monoacylglycerol + 2 fatty acids.)

prompt: Pancreatic lipase digests a triacylglycerol in the small intestine (an incomplete hydrolysis). What are the products?
why: Pancreatic lipase removes two fatty acids, and it frees fatty acids, not glycerol.

Acetyl CoA comes from β-oxidation inside cells, not from digestion.
explain: In the intestine only two ester bonds are hydrolyzed, leaving a monoacylglycerol. These are later recombined into triacylglycerols in the intestinal wall.

prompt:

Fatty acids become acetyl CoA, which can’t make net glucose.
Muscle lacks glucose 6-phosphatase, so its glycogen stays in the muscle.
hint: Only the liver shares its glycogen with the blood.
explain: Glucagon tells the liver to break down glycogen and release glucose. Muscle glycogen is kept for the muscle itself. As liver glycogen runs low, gluconeogenesis takes over.

prompt: Phosphofructokinase is an allosteric enzyme early in glycolysis, and ATP (a product of burning glucose) is one of its regulators. When the cell has plenty of ATP, what happens to phosphofructokinase?
choices: It runs backward to make glucose
It is inhibited, so glycolysis slows
It is activated, so glycolysis speeds up
answer: It is inhibited, so glycolysis slows
why: Glycolysis steps can’t run backward to make glucose. Gluconeogenesis uses different enzymes for the irreversible steps.
High ATP means the cell has plenty of energy, so it turns glycolysis down.
PFK is allosteric: ATP binds a regulatory site and inhibits it.
hint: Lots of energy already: speed up or slow down?
explain: High ATP inhibits phosphofructokinase (allosteric control): no need to burn more fuel. High ADP or AMP activates it.

prompt: After a meal, insulin is high. Which pathways does it switch on?
why: Those are fasting pathways, switched on by glucagon.
Those run when fat is the main fuel (fasting or no insulin).
Insulin blocks glycogen breakdown and ketone body production.
hint: Insulin = fed state = store.
explain: Insulin moves glucose into cells and promotes burning it and storing it (glycogen, fat). It also blocks fatty acids from entering mitochondria for β-oxidation.

prompt: When does the body run gluconeogenesis?
choices: When liver glycogen is low and blood glucose must be kept up, or to recycle lactate
Whenever ATP is high and insulin is high
answer: When liver glycogen is low and blood glucose must be kept up, or to recycle lactate
why: It runs whenever blood glucose needs support, day or night.
High ATP and insulin mean the fed state, when gluconeogenesis is turned off.
After a high-carb meal glucose is plentiful, so gluconeogenesis is off.
hint: It is expensive. When would you pay for it?
explain: Gluconeogenesis costs ATP, so it runs only when needed: refilling glycogen, recycling lactate and keeping blood glucose up during fasting.

prompt: What does allosteric control of an enzyme mean?
choices: The substrate binds the active site
A molecule binds the enzyme somewhere other than the active site and changes its activity
The enzyme is destroyed by heat
The enzyme is made from a vitamin
answer: A molecule binds the enzyme somewhere other than the active site and changes its activity
why: That describes normal substrate binding. Allosteric means a different site.
Heat denaturation is unfolding, not regulation.
Coenzymes come from vitamins, but that has nothing to do with allosteric control.
hint: allo- = other.
explain: An allosteric effector (like ATP or AMP on phosphofructokinase) binds a separate site and turns the enzyme up or down.

prompt: When a cell is active and uses ATP fast, what speeds up electron transport and ATP synthesis?
why: High ATP means the cell has enough energy, so electron transport slows.
O<sub style="font-size:13.8667px;line-height:0px">2</sub> is the final electron acceptor. Less O<sub style="font-size:13.8667px;line-height:0px">2</sub> slows electron transport.
NADH supplies the electrons. Less NADH slows electron transport.
hint: ATP synthase needs a raw material.
explain: Electron transport depends on ADP being available for ATP synthase. Low ADP, P<sub style="font-size:13.8667px;line-height:0px">i</sub>, O<sub style="font-size:13.8667px;line-height:0px">2</sub> or NADH slows it down.

prompt: Pyruvate kinase makes pyruvate and ATP in the last step of glycolysis, and pyruvate goes on to become acetyl CoA. Using feedback logic, high levels of which molecules most likely inhibit it?
why: ADP and AMP mean low energy, so they activate glycolysis.
Glucose is the starting fuel. More glucose doesn’t signal to stop.
NAD+ is needed for glycolysis to keep running. It doesn’t inhibit pyruvate kinase.
hint: Both signal “enough fuel already.”
explain: Plenty of ATP or acetyl CoA means there is no need to make more pyruvate.

prompt: During hard exercise, ADP and AMP pile up, a sign the cell is low on ATP. They bind the glycolysis enzyme phosphofructokinase at an allosteric site. What do they most likely do to it?
choices: Activate it, so glycolysis speeds up
answer: Activate it, so glycolysis speeds up
why: ADP and AMP signal low energy, so they speed up ATP production.
ADP and AMP are major allosteric regulators of PFK.
Allosteric effectors bind reversibly and change activity. They don’t destroy enzymes.
hint: Low energy: speed up or slow down?
explain: High ADP/AMP means the cell is low on ATP, so it activates PFK to make more.

prompt: Hexokinase turns glucose into glucose 6-phosphate. Like many enzymes, it is slowed by product (feedback) inhibition. High levels of which molecule inhibit it?
why: Glucose is the substrate, not the product.
Insulin is a hormone that acts through signaling, not a product of this step.
ADP is a product of the reaction, but feedback inhibition here comes from the sugar product.
hint: What does hexokinase make?
explain: When its product builds up, hexokinase slows down: product (feedback) inhibition.

prompt: Isocitrate dehydrogenase is a citric acid cycle step that makes NADH. Using feedback logic (product slows it; low energy speeds it up), which pair controls it?
choices: NAD<sup style="font-size:13.8667px;line-height:0px">+</sup> inhibits it; ATP activates it
FADH<sub style="font-size:13.8667px;line-height:0px">2</sub> inhibits it; O<sub style="font-size:13.8667px;line-height:0px">2</sub> activates it
Glucose inhibits it; insulin activates it
NADH inhibits it; ADP activates it
answer: NADH inhibits it; ADP activates it
why: NAD+ is a reactant the step needs. High ATP inhibits, not activates.
This step makes NADH, not FADH<sub style="font-size:13.8667px;line-height:0px">2</sub>, and O<sub style="font-size:13.8667px;line-height:0px">2</sub> doesn’t bind this enzyme.
This step responds to energy and NADH levels, not to glucose or insulin directly.
hint: It makes NADH.
explain: Lots of NADH (product) slows the step; ADP (low energy) speeds it up.

prompt: The citric acid cycle runs to supply ATP (through NADH and FADH2). Citrate synthase, its first enzyme, is regulated by the cell’s energy level. Which response makes sense?
choices: ATP activates it; ADP inhibits it
ATP inhibits it; ADP activates it
answer: ATP inhibits it; ADP activates it
why: The citric acid cycle is tightly regulated by the cell’s energy needs.
That is backwards. ATP is the product the cycle supplies, so plenty of ATP slows it.
The cycle responds to the cell’s energy level (ATP and ADP), not to glucose.
hint: Same logic as phosphofructokinase.
explain: The cycle runs at the rate the body needs ATP: high ATP slows it, high ADP speeds it up.

prompt: Which hormones trigger fat cells to hydrolyze stored triacylglycerols?
why: Insulin promotes fat storage. Thyroxine raises metabolic rate but isn’t the main trigger here.
Insulin blocks fat breakdown, so it can’t be one of the triggers.
Insulin signals the fed state and stops fat breakdown.
hint: Fasting and “fight or flight” hormones.
explain: Glucagon and epinephrine activate a lipase that releases glycerol and fatty acids into the blood. Insulin does the opposite.

prompt: Compare side chains: tyrosine is –CH2–C6H4–OH and phenylalanine is –CH2–C6H5. The nonessential amino acid tyrosine is made by adding an –OH to which amino acid?
why: Alanine’s side chain is just –CH<sub style="font-size:13.8667px;line-height:0px">3</sub>; it has no ring to add –OH to.
Glutamate has a –CH<sub style="font-size:13.8667px;line-height:0px">2</sub>CH<sub style="font-size:13.8667px;line-height:0px">2</sub>COO⁻ side chain, not a benzene ring.
Tryptophan has a different ring system (indole). Tyrosine’s ring matches phenylalanine’s.
explain: Phenylalanine hydroxylase oxidizes phenylalanine to tyrosine using O<sub style="font-size:13.8667px;line-height:0px">2</sub> and NADPH.

prompt: Which three sources make up the amino acid pool?
choices: Dietary protein, protein turnover and liver synthesis of nonessential amino acids
answer: Dietary protein, protein turnover and liver synthesis of nonessential amino acids
why: Protein turnover and liver synthesis also refill the pool.
These contain no nitrogen, so they can’t supply amino acids by themselves.
Glycogen and fat contain no nitrogen, and urea is a waste product.
explain: The pool is refilled by food, by breaking down old proteins (turnover) and by the liver making nonessential amino acids.

prompt: Amino acids whose carbon skeletons become pyruvate or citric acid cycle intermediates (so they can make glucose) are called:
why: Essential means the body can’t make it and must eat it. That says nothing about where the skeleton goes.
“Lipogenic” isn’t the term used for amino acid skeletons; the two classes are glucogenic and ketogenic.
Ketogenic amino acids become acetyl CoA or acetoacetyl CoA, which can’t make glucose.
explain: Glucogenic amino acids can feed gluconeogenesis. Ketogenic ones become acetyl CoA or acetoacetyl CoA (fat or ketone bodies).

prompt: Trypsin hydrolyzes the peptide bond on the carboxyl side of lysine (Lys) and arginine (Arg). What does trypsin make from the peptide Ala–Lys–Gly–Arg–Phe?
why: Trypsin also cuts after Arg, so Gly–Arg–Phe is split again.
Trypsin cuts after Lys and Arg (their carboxyl side), not before them.
Trypsin cuts only after Lys and Arg, not every peptide bond.
hint: Carboxyl side = the bond to the right of Lys and Arg (N-terminal on the left).
explain: Cut after Lys (between Lys and Gly) and after Arg (between Arg and Phe): Ala–Lys + Gly–Arg + Phe. Each cut is a hydrolysis that uses one H<sub style="font-size:13.8667px;line-height:0px">2</sub>O.

prompt: Amino acids whose carbon skeletons become acetyl CoA or acetoacetyl CoA are called:
why: Nonessential means the body can make it. That is a different question.
Glucogenic skeletons become pyruvate or cycle intermediates, which can make glucose.
“Glycolytic” isn’t a class of amino acids. Acetyl CoA products make them ketogenic.
explain: Acetyl CoA cannot make net glucose, so these amino acids can only make fatty acids or ketone bodies.

prompt: Dietary protein is used mainly to build and repair body proteins, and only a small share is burned for fuel. About how much of the body’s energy comes from protein?
why: Some amino acids are burned, about 10% of energy.
About 50% is far too high; carbohydrates and fats supply most energy.
90% is far too high; protein is mainly for building.
explain: Proteins mainly supply amino acids for building; only about 10% of energy comes from them.

prompt: In the stomach, what does HCl do to dietary protein?
choices: Hydrolyzes it into single amino acids
Denatures it and activates pepsinogen into pepsin
Nothing; protein digestion starts in the mouth
answer: Denatures it and activates pepsinogen into pepsin
why: HCl unfolds proteins but doesn’t cut them into single amino acids. Pepsin and later proteases do the cutting.
Urea is made in the liver from amino acid nitrogen, not by stomach acid.
Saliva has no protease. Protein digestion starts in the stomach.
explain: HCl unfolds proteins and turns on pepsin, which cuts proteins into polypeptides.

prompt: Before an amino acid can be burned for energy, what must happen first?
choices: Its amino nitrogen must be removed
It must be joined into a protein
It must be turned into glucose
answer: Its amino nitrogen must be removed
why: Joining into a protein is building, not burning.
Phosphorylation isn’t the required first step for amino acids. Removing the amino group is.
Some skeletons can become glucose, but the nitrogen must come off first.
explain: The body cannot oxidize nitrogen-containing compounds, so the N is removed (ending up as urea) and the carbon skeleton is used.

prompt: Use the urea cycle diagram. Which two molecules link it to the citric acid cycle?
why: NH<sub style="font-size:13.8667px;line-height:0px">4</sub>+ enters as carbamoyl phosphate, and urea leaves the body. Neither joins the citric acid cycle.
Ornithine and citrulline cycle within the urea cycle; they don’t link to the citric acid cycle.
Arginine is a urea cycle intermediate. Glutamate supplies N through transamination, but the direct links are aspartate and fumarate.
explain: Aspartate brings in the second N (made from oxaloacetate), and fumarate leaves to rejoin the citric acid cycle.

prompt:
A teenager is growing fast. More protein is being built than broken down.

What is their nitrogen balance?
choices: Nitrogen balance does not apply to growth
why: Negative balance means breakdown exceeds synthesis (starvation, wasting illness). Growth is the opposite.
Growth is a classic case of positive nitrogen balance.
Zero balance is a steady adult: synthesis and breakdown are equal. Growth builds more than it breaks.
explain: Positive balance: protein synthesis exceeds breakdown (growth, pregnancy, recovering from illness).

prompt: Why must essential amino acids come from food?
choices: They are only found in plants
They contain too much nitrogen to make
The body lacks the pathways to build their carbon skeletons
answer: The body lacks the pathways to build their carbon skeletons
why: Animal proteins like meat, eggs and milk are rich in essential amino acids.
The nitrogen comes easily by transamination. The carbon skeleton is the hard part.
The liver doesn’t destroy them. We simply can’t make them.
explain: Essential amino acids need many more reaction steps than we have enzymes for; nonessential ones are made in a few steps.

prompt: Transamination turns a keto acid into an amino acid with the same carbon skeleton. Pyruvate (3 C), oxaloacetate (4 C) and α-ketoglutarate (5 C) are keto acids from glycolysis and the citric acid cycle. Which three nonessential amino acids do they become?
why: Tyrosine is made from phenylalanine. Serine and glycine come from a glycolysis intermediate (3-phosphoglycerate), not these keto acids.
Lysine, leucine and valine are essential: we can’t make them.
Ornithine and citrulline are urea cycle intermediates, not amino acids used to build proteins.
explain: Pyruvate → alanine, oxaloacetate → aspartate, α-ketoglutarate → glutamate, each by transamination.

prompt:
A pregnant patient is building new tissue every day.

What is her nitrogen balance?
why: Zero balance means no net gain, but pregnancy keeps adding tissue.
Negative balance means losing protein. Pregnancy builds new tissue.
Building new tissue every day means positive nitrogen balance.
explain: Pregnancy builds new tissue, so N taken in exceeds N excreted: positive balance.

prompt:
A patient with a wasting illness is losing muscle. More protein is being broken down than built.

What is their nitrogen balance?
choices: Nitrogen balance does not apply to illness
why: Wasting illness is a classic case of negative nitrogen balance.
Positive balance means building more than breaking down, as in growth or pregnancy.
Zero means synthesis equals breakdown. Losing muscle means breakdown is winning.
explain: Negative balance: protein breakdown exceeds synthesis (starvation, protein-poor diet, wasting illness).

prompt:
Nursing: a patient in septic shock has poor blood flow, and their blood lactate is rising.

Why?
choices: Lactate is made by the kidneys during shock
The liver is making extra lactate from glycogen
Lactate comes from breaking down fat
Tissues are short of O<sub style="font-size:13.8667px;line-height:0px">2</sub>, so they switch to lactic acid fermentation
answer: Tissues are short of O<sub style="font-size:13.8667px;line-height:0px">2</sub>, so they switch to lactic acid fermentation
why: The kidneys help clear lactate. They aren’t the source.
The liver normally clears lactate. It doesn’t make extra from glycogen during shock.
Fat breakdown gives acetyl CoA and ketone bodies, not lactate.
hint: What does a muscle do without O<sub style="font-size:13.75px;line-height:0px">2</sub>?
explain: Without enough O<sub style="font-size:13.8667px;line-height:0px">2</sub>, NADH cannot be recycled by electron transport, so pyruvate is reduced to lactate. High lactate is a warning sign of poor oxygen delivery.

prompt:
Dental hygiene: during a cleaning you notice a fruity, nail-polish smell on a patient’s breath. They mention they have diabetes.

What molecule is likely causing the smell, and where did it come from?
choices: Acetone, from ketogenesis in the liver when fat is being burned heavily
Ethanol, from yeast in the mouth
answer: Acetone, from ketogenesis in the liver when fat is being burned heavily
why: Urea doesn’t give a fruity smell, and the kidneys excrete it rather than make it.
Lactate isn’t volatile and doesn’t smell fruity.
Ethanol isn’t a typical sign of diabetes, and the mouth doesn’t normally ferment it.
hint: Which ketone body is volatile?
explain: Acetone forms when acetoacetate loses CO<sub style="font-size:13.8667px;line-height:0px">2</sub>. It is volatile, so it is exhaled. It can be a sign of poorly controlled diabetes and should be reported.

prompt:
Nursing: a patient in diabetic ketoacidosis is breathing deeply and quickly. (CO2 in the blood forms carbonic acid, H2CO3.)

Why?
choices: The brain is out of glucose and stops controlling breathing
Ketone bodies are gases that must be exhaled
Acidic ketone bodies have lowered blood pH, and fast breathing removes CO<sub style="font-size:13.8667px;line-height:0px">2</sub> to raise the pH
answer: Acidic ketone bodies have lowered blood pH, and fast breathing removes CO<sub style="font-size:13.8667px;line-height:0px">2</sub> to raise the pH
why: The breathing is a response to acidic blood, not a loss of brain control.
Ketone bodies are dissolved acids. Only acetone is volatile, and it isn’t why breathing speeds up.
Ketone bodies are in the blood, not the airways.
hint: Ketone bodies are acids.
explain: Ketoacidosis lowers blood pH. Breathing off CO<sub style="font-size:13.8667px;line-height:0px">2</sub> (an acid in blood) partly compensates. Other signs: acetone breath, frequent urination, dehydration.

prompt:
Nursing: a patient had their gallbladder removed and now has trouble with very fatty meals. (The gallbladder stores bile, made by the liver, and squeezes it out at mealtime.)

Why?
choices: Bile salts hydrolyze fats by themselves
The gallbladder stores glycogen for fat digestion
Less bile salt arrives at once to emulsify fat, so pancreatic lipase has less surface to work on
answer: Less bile salt arrives at once to emulsify fat, so pancreatic lipase has less surface to work on
why: The pancreas makes lipase. The gallbladder only stores bile.
Bile salts only emulsify fat. Lipase does the hydrolysis.
The gallbladder stores bile, not glycogen.
hint: Bile salts emulsify; lipase hydrolyzes.
explain: Bile salts act like soap, breaking fat globules into micelles so the water-soluble lipase can reach the ester bonds. The liver still makes bile, but without storage less is released at mealtime.

prompt:
Nursing: a patient with severe liver failure becomes confused, and their blood ammonia is high.

Why is ammonia high?
choices: Glycolysis makes ammonia when the liver fails
The urea cycle runs in the liver, so NH<sub style="font-size:13.8667px;line-height:0px">4</sub><sup style="font-size:13.8667px;line-height:0px">+</sup> is not turned into urea
Ammonia comes from too much glucose
answer: The urea cycle runs in the liver, so NH<sub style="font-size:13.8667px;line-height:0px">4</sub><sup style="font-size:13.8667px;line-height:0px">+</sup> is not turned into urea
why: Glycolysis contains no nitrogen, so it can’t make ammonia.
The kidneys excrete urea; they aren’t the source of the ammonia.
Glucose has no nitrogen, so it can’t become ammonia.
hint: Where is urea made?
explain: The liver is where NH<sub style="font-size:13.8667px;line-height:0px">4</sub>+ is packed into urea. Without it, toxic ammonia builds up and affects the brain.

prompt:
Nursing: a patient with uncontrolled type 1 diabetes gives a urine sample for a dipstick test.

Which two results would you expect to be positive?
why: Lactate isn’t a typical dipstick finding in diabetes.
Protein in urine points to kidney damage, and urea is always in urine.
Glycogen and fatty acids aren’t found in urine.
hint: Think of what builds up in the blood without insulin.
explain: Blood glucose is so high that it spills into the urine, and fat burning without insulin makes ketone bodies, which are water soluble and also appear in urine.

prompt:
Nursing: a patient has acute pancreatitis.

Which digestive enzymes are made by the pancreas, so digestion in the small intestine suffers?
why: Lactase and sucrase are on the small intestine’s own lining.
Pepsin and HCl come from the stomach.
Salivary amylase comes from the salivary glands, not the pancreas.
hint: Which enzymes are named “pancreatic”?
explain: The pancreas sends amylase (starch), lipase (fats) and trypsin/chymotrypsin (proteins) into the small intestine, so all three food types are affected. Pepsin and HCl come from the stomach.

prompt:
Dental hygiene: a patient asks why xylitol gum is recommended. Xylitol is a sugar alcohol that tastes sweet, but plaque bacteria cannot break it down for energy.

Why does xylitol gum help prevent cavities?
choices: Xylitol is fermented to a base
Xylitol coats the teeth with fat
Plaque bacteria cannot ferment xylitol into acid
answer: Plaque bacteria cannot ferment xylitol into acid
why: Xylitol isn’t fermented at all, so nothing is made from it.
Xylitol is a sugar alcohol, not a fat, and it doesn’t coat teeth.
Xylitol doesn’t sterilize the mouth. Bacteria just can’t use it.
hint: Acid comes from fermentation.
explain: Xylitol is a sugar alcohol that cavity-causing bacteria cannot ferment, so no lactic acid is made.

prompt:
Nursing: a newborn screening test is positive for PKU. The baby lacks phenylalanine hydroxylase, the enzyme that converts phenylalanine into tyrosine.

What happens, and how is it managed?
choices: Tyrosine builds up, so tyrosine is removed from the diet
Glucose builds up, so insulin is given
Urea builds up, so protein is increased
Phenylalanine builds up (it cannot become tyrosine), so the baby needs a low-phenylalanine diet
answer: Phenylalanine builds up (it cannot become tyrosine), so the baby needs a low-phenylalanine diet
why: Tyrosine can’t be made without the enzyme, so it doesn’t build up.
PKU is about an amino acid, not blood glucose.
PKU doesn’t raise urea, and more protein would make it worse (more phenylalanine).
hint: Which reaction is missing?
explain: Phenylalanine hydroxylase normally oxidizes phenylalanine to tyrosine. Without it, phenylalanine accumulates and harms the developing brain, so the diet limits it (and aspartame).

prompt:
Nursing: a patient with long-term alcohol use is low in thiamine (vitamin B1). Thiamine is made into the coenzyme TPP, which helps remove CO2 in oxidative decarboxylations.

Which step of energy production is hurt most?
choices: The electron transport chain at complex IV
Removing CO<sub style="font-size:13.8667px;line-height:0px">2</sub> from pyruvate (pyruvate → acetyl CoA) and α-ketoglutarate
answer: Removing CO<sub style="font-size:13.8667px;line-height:0px">2</sub> from pyruvate (pyruvate → acetyl CoA) and α-ketoglutarate
why: Complex IV uses copper and heme iron, not thiamine.
Glycolysis step 1 uses hexokinase and ATP, not TPP.
Fatty acid activation uses ATP and coenzyme A, not TPP.
hint: TPP helps remove CO<sub style="font-size:13.75px;line-height:0px">2</sub>.
explain: Thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP) is needed for the oxidative decarboxylations of pyruvate and α-ketoglutarate, so glucose cannot be fully burned.

prompt:
Anatomy & physiology: mature red blood cells have no mitochondria.

How do they make ATP, and what do they release?
choices: The citric acid cycle, releasing CO<sub style="font-size:13.8667px;line-height:0px">2</sub>
why: Electron transport is in the inner mitochondrial membrane.
β-Oxidation is in mitochondria too.
The citric acid cycle is in mitochondria, which red blood cells lack.
hint: Which pathways happen in the cytosol?
explain: With no mitochondria, there is no citric acid cycle or electron transport. Red blood cells reduce pyruvate to lactate to recycle NAD+, and the liver turns that lactate back into glucose (Cori cycle).

prompt:
Anatomy & physiology: both the liver and skeletal muscle store glycogen. Breaking glycogen down gives glucose 6-phosphate, and a phosphorylated sugar cannot cross the cell membrane.

Why can only the liver release glucose into the blood?
choices: Glucose cannot cross a muscle cell membrane in either direction
Only the liver has glucose 6-phosphatase to remove the phosphate, so muscle keeps its glucose 6-phosphate for itself
Muscle cells have no glycogen phosphorylase
Muscle glycogen is a different polymer that cannot be broken down
answer: Only the liver has glucose 6-phosphatase to remove the phosphate, so muscle keeps its glucose 6-phosphate for itself
why: Glucose can enter muscle cells (with insulin). The problem is getting it back out as glucose 6-phosphate.
Muscle does have glycogen phosphorylase; it breaks glycogen down for its own use.
Muscle glycogen is the same polymer as liver glycogen.
hint: What enzyme removes the phosphate?
explain: Glycogenolysis gives glucose 6-phosphate, which is trapped in the cell. The liver’s glucose 6-phosphatase (a hydrolase) frees glucose for the blood; muscle uses its glucose 6-phosphate in glycolysis.

prompt:
Nursing: a patient gets bloating, cramps and gas after drinking milk. They are low in the enzyme lactase.

What is happening?
choices: The liver cannot turn galactose into glucose
Lactose is hydrolyzed too quickly into galactose
Lactose is not hydrolyzed in the small intestine, so bacteria in the colon ferment it and make gas
Milk protein is not digested in the stomach
answer: Lactose is not hydrolyzed in the small intestine, so bacteria in the colon ferment it and make gas
why: The problem is in the gut, before anything reaches the liver.
Without lactase, lactose isn’t hydrolyzed at all.
Lactose is a sugar, not a protein.
hint: Lactase is a hydrolase on the small intestine wall.
explain: Lactase (a hydrolase) normally splits lactose into glucose and galactose for absorption. Undigested lactose feeds colon bacteria, whose fermentation makes gas and draws in water.

prompt:
Dental hygiene: a patient sips soda all day and has new cavities.

How does the sugar cause tooth decay?
choices: Salivary amylase turns sugar into an acid
Plaque bacteria ferment the sugar to lactic acid, which lowers the pH and dissolves enamel
Sugar is oxidized to CO<sub style="font-size:13.8667px;line-height:0px">2</sub>, which etches the tooth
answer: Plaque bacteria ferment the sugar to lactic acid, which lowers the pH and dissolves enamel
why: Amylase breaks starch into sugars. It doesn’t make acid.
Sugar is neutral. It is the acid bacteria make from it that dissolves enamel.
Bacteria in plaque ferment sugar to lactic acid. They don’t oxidize it to CO<sub style="font-size:13.8667px;line-height:0px">2</sub>.
hint: Bacteria in plaque have little O<sub style="font-size:13.75px;line-height:0px">2</sub>.
explain: Bacteria like Streptococcus mutans run glycolysis and lactic acid fermentation. Frequent sugar keeps the plaque acidic, so enamel keeps losing minerals.

prompt:
During hard sprints, a student’s leg muscles burn and tire because O2 cannot be delivered fast enough.

What builds up in the muscle?
choices: Lactate, from anaerobic metabolism of pyruvate
answer: Lactate, from anaerobic metabolism of pyruvate
why: Ketone bodies come from fat breakdown in the liver during fasting.
Urea comes from amino acid nitrogen in the liver.
Glycogen is being used up during sprints, not built.
hint: Not enough O<sub style="font-size:13.75px;line-height:0px">2</sub> for the ATP demand.
explain: When O<sub style="font-size:13.8667px;line-height:0px">2</sub> cannot keep up, pyruvate is reduced to lactate. Deep breathing later lets the body oxidize lactate back to pyruvate.

prompt:
Nursing: a patient on insulin skipped lunch and is now shaky and confused. Blood glucose is 45 mg/dL.

Why does the brain show symptoms first?
choices: The brain burns protein instead of glucose
The brain depends almost entirely on blood glucose and cannot use fatty acids for fuel
The brain stores large amounts of glycogen that run out first
Low glucose makes the brain produce ketone bodies
answer: The brain depends almost entirely on blood glucose and cannot use fatty acids for fuel
why: The brain runs on glucose, not protein.
The brain stores very little glycogen.
The brain uses ketone bodies but doesn’t make them, and that only helps after days of fasting.
hint: Which fuels can reach the brain?
explain: Fatty acids cannot cross into the brain, and the brain stores very little glycogen, so a sudden drop in blood glucose affects it first. (Ketone bodies only help after days of fasting.)

prompt:
Dental hygiene: crackers stuck between the molars turn sweet after a few minutes.

Which enzyme is breaking the starch into sugars there?
why: Pepsin works on proteins in the stomach, not starch in the mouth.
Trypsin digests proteins in the small intestine.
Pancreatic lipase digests fats in the small intestine.
hint: Starch digestion starts in the mouth.
explain: Salivary amylase hydrolyzes starch in the mouth, which also feeds the plaque bacteria.

prompt:
Nursing: a patient with kidney failure has a high BUN (blood urea nitrogen).

Why does urea build up?
choices: The liver keeps making urea, but the kidneys cannot excrete it in urine
Urea is made from glucose when the kidneys fail
The kidneys run the urea cycle and it has stopped
answer: The liver keeps making urea, but the kidneys cannot excrete it in urine
why: Urea leaves in urine. The lungs exhale CO<sub style="font-size:13.8667px;line-height:0px">2</sub> and acetone, not urea.
Urea comes from amino acid nitrogen, not from glucose.
The urea cycle is in the liver.
hint: Which organ makes urea, and which removes it?
explain: Urea is made in the liver (urea cycle) and removed by the kidneys. Kidney failure lets it accumulate in the blood.

prompt:
A toddler swallows rubbing alcohol (isopropyl alcohol).

What will the child’s breath smell of, and why?
choices: Formaldehyde, because it becomes an aldehyde
Vinegar, because it becomes acetic acid
Nothing, because isopropyl alcohol is not metabolized
Acetone, because the 2° alcohol is oxidized to a ketone that cannot be oxidized further
answer: Acetone, because the 2° alcohol is oxidized to a ketone that cannot be oxidized further
why: An aldehyde comes from a 1° alcohol. The –OH here is on the middle carbon.
Vinegar (acetic acid) comes from a 1° alcohol like ethanol. Isopropyl alcohol is 2°.
Alcohol dehydrogenase oxidizes it, giving acetone.
hint: Is it a 1°, 2° or 3° alcohol?
explain: Alcohol dehydrogenase turns isopropyl alcohol into acetone, which is exhaled, the same compound behind the fruity breath of ketoacidosis.

prompt:
Someone on a very strict diet has headaches, a dry mouth and acetone-smelling breath.

What is happening?
choices: Ketosis: ketone bodies are building up because fat is the main fuel
answer: Ketosis: ketone bodies are building up because fat is the main fuel
why: Strict dieting empties glycogen stores rather than filling them.
Lactic acidosis comes from O<sub style="font-size:13.8667px;line-height:0px">2</sub> shortage in hard exercise, and lactate has no acetone smell.
Strict dieting tends to break protein down, the opposite of positive balance.
hint: Fruity or acetone breath is the clue.
explain: Starvation, vigorous dieting, alcoholism and uncontrolled diabetes all push fat breakdown, so ketone bodies build up. Severe cases become ketoacidosis.

prompt:
Nursing: a patient recovering from surgery is on a high-protein diet while the wound heals.

What is their nitrogen balance?
choices: Positive: more protein is being built than broken down
Negative: more protein is being broken down than built
Zero: nitrogen in equals nitrogen out
Nitrogen balance does not apply after surgery
answer: Positive: more protein is being built than broken down
why: Negative balance means breakdown is winning. Healing builds tissue.
Zero means no net gain, but healing adds new tissue.
Recovery from surgery is a classic case of positive balance.
hint: Is the body building tissue?
explain: Recovery (convalescence) builds new tissue, so more nitrogen is kept than excreted: positive nitrogen balance.

prompt:
Nursing: a liver function panel shows a high blood level of ALT (alanine transaminase), an enzyme normally found inside liver cells.

What does that suggest, and what does ALT normally do?
choices: The patient ate too much protein; ALT digests protein in the stomach
The kidneys are making too much urea
Liver cells are damaged and leaking ALT, an enzyme that transfers an amino group from alanine to α-ketoglutarate
Blood glucose is high; ALT makes glucose from glycogen
answer: Liver cells are damaged and leaking ALT, an enzyme that transfers an amino group from alanine to α-ketoglutarate
why: ALT works inside liver cells. It doesn’t digest protein in the stomach.
High ALT points to the liver, not the kidneys, and urea is a different test (BUN).
ALT is a transaminase that moves amino groups. It doesn’t make glucose from glycogen.
hint: Transaminases work inside cells, not in the blood.
explain: ALT is a transferase that runs transamination inside liver cells. When liver cells are injured, it leaks into the blood, so a high blood level is a sign of liver damage.

prompt: Glycolysis makes ATP, and ATP acts as a feedback regulator of the glycolysis enzyme phosphofructokinase. When ATP levels in a cell are high, phosphofructokinase is ________ and glycolysis ________.
explain: High ATP inhibits phosphofructokinase (allosteric control): the cell does not need to break down more glucose.

prompt: In transamination, the C=O of a keto acid becomes C–NH3+ and the carbon skeleton stays the same. Oxaloacetate, ⁻OOC–CO–CH2–COO⁻, undergoes transamination. Which amino acid is made?
explain: Same 4-carbon skeleton with two carboxylates: ⁻OOC–CH(NH<sub style="font-size:13.8667px;line-height:0px">3</sub>+)–CH<sub style="font-size:13.8667px;line-height:0px">2</sub>–COO⁻ is aspartate. (Pyruvate → alanine and α-ketoglutarate → glutamate the same way.)

prompt: How many electrons are passed along when one FADH2 is oxidized back to FAD in complex II?
explain: FADH<sub style="font-size:13.8667px;line-height:0px">2</sub> carries 2 H atoms, which is 2 electrons (plus 2 H+).

prompt: Palmitoleic acid has 16 carbons and one cis double bond. Each turn of β-oxidation normally makes 1 FADH2, but a C=C already in the chain skips one FAD step. How many FADH2 does its β-oxidation make?
explain: 16 carbons → 7 turns. The existing C=C skips one FAD step, so 7 − 1 = 6 FADH<sub style="font-size:13.8667px;line-height:0px">2</sub>.

prompt: In glycolysis, one step splits a six-carbon sugar into two three-carbon sugars without using water or ATP. This step is catalyzed by
explain: Step 4: aldolase cleaves fructose 1,6-bisphosphate into DHAP and glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate without water or ATP, so it is a lyase.

prompt: In the electron transport chain, the O2 we breathe in ends up as
explain: At complex IV, electrons and H+ combine with O<sub style="font-size:13.8667px;line-height:0px">2</sub> to make water. The CO<sub style="font-size:13.8667px;line-height:0px">2</sub> we breathe out comes from the citric acid cycle and pyruvate oxidation.

prompt: Using 2.5 ATP per NADH and 1.5 ATP per FADH2, the complete oxidation of one glucose yields
explain: Glycolysis 7 + pyruvate oxidation 5 + two turns of the cycle 20 = 32 ATP. (38 uses the older 3 and 2 values.)

prompt: Which process does NOT take place in the mitochondrial matrix?
explain: Glycolysis runs in the cytosol. The other four are in the matrix.

prompt: In gluconeogenesis, fructose 1,6-bisphosphate + H2O → fructose 6-phosphate + Pi. Which type of enzyme is most likely used?
explain: Water removes the phosphate, so a phosphatase (hydrolase) is used. This bypasses the irreversible phosphofructokinase step.

prompt: Which coenzyme is made from pantothenic acid (vitamin B5)?
explain: Coenzyme A contains pantothenic acid; its –SH group carries acetyl and acyl groups.

prompt: Amino acids whose carbon skeletons are degraded to acetyl CoA are called
explain: Acetyl CoA can become fatty acids or ketone bodies but not net glucose, so these amino acids are ketogenic.

prompt: Lactate builds up in muscle during strenuous exercise because
choices: too much O<sub style="font-size:13.8667px;line-height:0px">2</sub> reaches the muscle
O<sub style="font-size:13.8667px;line-height:0px">2</sub> is not supplied fast enough to reoxidize NADH in the electron transport chain
answer: O<sub style="font-size:13.8667px;line-height:0px">2</sub> is not supplied fast enough to reoxidize NADH in the electron transport chain
explain: Without enough O<sub style="font-size:13.8667px;line-height:0px">2</sub>, NADH piles up; reducing pyruvate to lactate regenerates NAD+ so glycolysis can continue.

prompt: Which statement about glycerol released from a triacylglycerol is TRUE?
choices: It is broken down by β-oxidation.
It is converted directly to urea.
It is converted to dihydroxyacetone phosphate, which can enter glycolysis or gluconeogenesis.
It cannot be used for energy.
It is turned into ketone bodies.
answer: It is converted to dihydroxyacetone phosphate, which can enter glycolysis or gluconeogenesis.
explain: Glycerol is phosphorylated and then oxidized to DHAP, an intermediate of both pathways.

prompt: The coenzyme FAD is reduced to FADH2 when a ________ bond in the substrate becomes a ________ bond.
explain: FAD dehydrogenates –CH<sub style="font-size:13.8667px;line-height:0px">2</sub>–CH<sub style="font-size:13.8667px;line-height:0px">2</sub>– to –CH=CH– (succinate → fumarate, β-oxidation step 1). NAD+ handles C–O oxidations.

prompt: Glycogenolysis is a(n) ________ pathway and glycogenesis is a(n) ________ pathway.
explain: Glycogenolysis breaks glycogen down (catabolic); glycogenesis builds it (anabolic).

prompt: An enzyme that removes CO2 from a substrate without using ATP, water or a coenzyme to split it is classified as a(an)
explain: Decarboxylases break a C–C bond without water or ATP, so they are lyases.

prompt: The positive charge in NAD+ is located on the
choices: nitrogen of the nicotinamide ring, which has 4 bonds
answer: nitrogen of the nicotinamide ring, which has 4 bonds
explain: The nicotinamide N makes 4 bonds instead of 3, so it carries the + charge.

prompt: Which coenzyme accepts the hydrogens when malate (a 2° alcohol) is oxidized to oxaloacetate (a ketone)?
explain: None of these: the answer is NAD<sup style="font-size:13.8667px;line-height:0px">+</sup>, which oxidizes 2° alcohols to ketones and becomes NADH.

prompt: Each turn of the citric acid cycle releases ________ CO2 and makes ________ NADH.
explain: Two decarboxylations release 2 CO<sub style="font-size:13.8667px;line-height:0px">2</sub>; three NAD+ oxidations make 3 NADH (plus 1 FADH<sub style="font-size:13.8667px;line-height:0px">2</sub> and 1 GTP).

prompt: What is the product when CH3–CH(OH)–CH2–COO⁻ is oxidized by NAD+?
explain: NAD+ oxidizes the 2° alcohol to a ketone: β-hydroxybutyrate → acetoacetate.

prompt: Which statement about NADPH is TRUE?
choices: It is the final electron acceptor of the electron transport chain.
It is made by the pentose phosphate pathway and used to build fatty acids.
It is the oxidized form of NADP<sup style="font-size:13.8667px;line-height:0px">+</sup>.

answer: It is made by the pentose phosphate pathway and used to build fatty acids.
explain: NADPH is the reducing agent for biosynthesis such as lipogenesis; the pentose phosphate pathway makes it.

prompt: Ketone bodies are made in the ________ when ________ builds up faster than the citric acid cycle can use it.
explain: Liver mitochondria turn excess acetyl CoA (from heavy β-oxidation) into acetoacetate, β-hydroxybutyrate and acetone.

prompt: Which pathway converts acetyl CoA into fatty acids in the cytosol using NADPH?
explain: Lipogenesis builds fatty acids 2 carbons at a time (from malonyl ACP), using NADPH, in the cytosol.

prompt: Use the urea cycle diagram. Which pair of molecules leaves the urea cycle as products?
explain: Urea goes to the kidneys and fumarate goes to the citric acid cycle. Ornithine is made again and stays in the cycle; aspartate goes in.

prompt: In R–CH2–CH2–CO–S–CoA → R–CH=CH–CO–S–CoA, the substrate is ________ and FAD is ________.
explain: The substrate loses 2 H (oxidized) and FAD gains them, becoming FADH<sub style="font-size:13.8667px;line-height:0px">2</sub> (reduced).

prompt: A saturated fatty acid with 12 carbons gives ________ acetyl CoA in ________ turns of β-oxidation.
explain: 12 ÷ 2 = 6 acetyl CoA. The last turn releases two at once, so 6 − 1 = 5 turns.

prompt: Hydrolysis of ATP to ADP + Pi is ________, so it is coupled to reactions that ________ energy.
explain: ATP hydrolysis releases energy, which drives energy-requiring (unfavorable) reactions such as phosphorylating glucose.
